title: Singular integrals: a starter
html:
We begin with the simpliest subject of our current theme of study, namely the Hilbert transform. It often appears in two forms. One is as a Fourier multiplier operator: in the case the underlying space is R {\mathbb{R}}R,

H(f)(x)=∫Rf∧(ξ)sign(ξ)ie2πixξ dξ\displaystyle H(f)(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f^{\wedge}(\xi)\frac{\text{sign}(\xi)}{i}e^{2\pi ix\xi}\thinspace d\xiH(f)(x)=∫R​f∧(ξ)isign(ξ)​e2πixξdξ

for f∈L2(R) {f\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}f∈L2(R), where

sign(ξ)={1ξ>00ξ=0−1ξ<0;f∧(ξ):=∫Rf(x)e−2πiξx dx\displaystyle \text{sign}(\xi)=\begin{cases} 1 & \xi>0\\ 0 & \xi=0\\ -1 & \xi<0 \end{cases}; f^{\wedge}(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\,dxsign(ξ)=⎩⎨⎧​10−1​ξ>0ξ=0ξ<0​;f∧(ξ):=∫R​f(x)e−2πiξxdx

or in the case the underlying space is a circle T {\mathbb{T}}T,

H(f)(θ)=∑n∈Zf∧(n)sign(n)ieinθ\displaystyle H(f)(\theta)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f^{\wedge}(n)\frac{\text{sign}(n)}{i}e^{in\theta}H(f)(θ)=n∈Z∑​f∧(n)isign(n)​einθ

where f∈L2([0,2π]) {f\in L^{2}([0,2\pi])}f∈L2([0,2π]), and

sign(n)={1n>00n=0−1n<0;f∧(n):=12π∫[0,2π]f(x)e−inx dx.\displaystyle \text{sign}(n)=\begin{cases} 1 & n>0\\ 0 & n=0\\ -1 & n<0 \end{cases}; f^{\wedge}(n):=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{[0,2\pi]}f(x)e^{-inx}\,dx.sign(n)=⎩⎨⎧​10−1​n>0n=0n<0​;f∧(n):=2π1​∫[0,2π]​f(x)e−inxdx.

(Note that the sign function vanishes on a measure zero set on R {\mathbb{R}}R, but on a measure 1 set on Z {\mathbb{Z}}Z. This ultimately causes the constant mode of the periodic function jumping out in various identities, compared to their analogs for functions on R {\mathbb{R}}R. This is however not essential.) The other formulation is as a "singular integral operator'', as will be ellaborated below. It is in the 19th and earlier 20th centuries that the properties of this operator came into interest, for its fundamental connection with the following two questions that arised in Analysis.

The first one is that of convergence, in some appropriate sense, of the symmetric partial sum of the Fourier series of an integrable function f:[0,2π]→C {f:[0,2\pi]\rightarrow\mathbb{C}}f:[0,2π]→C

SN(f)(θ):=∑∣n∣≤Nf∧(n)einθ→f(θ)?\displaystyle S_{N}(f)(\theta):=\sum_{|n|\leq N}f^{\wedge}(n)e^{in\theta}\rightarrow f(\theta) ?SN​(f)(θ):=∣n∣≤N∑​f∧(n)einθ→f(θ)?

At that time Lebesgue's integration theory had not been developed. However, that under the condition of C1 {C^{1}}C1 regularity of the function, the pointwise convergence was already clear to Dirichlet, in 1829, who told in private that he would soon resolve the case when f {f}f is continuous. This was disproved in 1873, by du Bois Reymond. Then after the work of Lebesgue, under the condition of square integrability of f {f}f, the L2 {L^{2}}L2 convergence can be established using elemental Hilbert space technique, invented during the end of the 19th century. Later, achieved by Marcel Riesz in 1923, the Lp {L^{p}}Lp convergence was shown to be true for all 1<p<∞ {1<p<\infty}1<p<∞. Nevertheless, the "local'' convergence behavior turns out much more intricate, and the a.e. convergence for L2 {L^{2}}L2 functions was eventually resolved by Carleson, in 1966.

The Hilbert transform enters the above question as follows. The symmetric partial sum can be regarded as the convolution with the Dirichlet kernel (this is no incidence: a bounded multiplier must correspond to a distributional kernel that commutes with translations)

SN(f)(θ)=f∗DN (θ),\displaystyle S_{N}(f)(\theta)=f*D_{N}\thinspace(\theta),SN​(f)(θ)=f∗DN​(θ),

where

DN(x)=∑∣n∣≤Neinx.\displaystyle D_{N}(x)=\sum_{|n|\leq N}e^{inx}.DN​(x)=∣n∣≤N∑​einx.

The integral operator so defined is actually the orthogonal projection P∣n∣≤N {P_{|n|\leq N}}P∣n∣≤N​ to the space spanned by {einx}∣n∣≤N {\{e^{inx}\}_{|n|\leq N}}{einx}∣n∣≤N​, which is associated with the following multiplier on the intergers

mSN(n)=χ∣n∣≤N={1∣n∣≤N0otherwise.\displaystyle m_{S_{N}}(n)=\chi_{|n|\leq N}=\begin{cases} 1 & |n|\leq N\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}.mSN​​(n)=χ∣n∣≤N​={10​∣n∣≤Notherwise​.

Denote the multiplier of the Hilber transform on the circle by mH(n):=1isign(n) {m_{H}(n):=\frac{1}{i}\text{sign}(n)}mH​(n):=i1​sign(n). And notice that

mSN(n)=i2(mH(n+N)−mH(n−N))+12χ{±N}.\displaystyle m_{S_{N}}(n)=\frac{i}{2}\left(m_{H}(n+N)-m_{H}(n-N)\right)+\frac{1}{2}\chi_{\{\pm N\}}.mSN​​(n)=2i​(mH​(n+N)−mH​(n−N))+21​χ{±N}​.

Then, in terms of operator,

SN(f)(θ)=ie−iNθH(eiNθf)−ieiNθH(e−iNθf)2+P±N2.\displaystyle S_{N}(f)(\theta)=\frac{ie^{-iN\theta}H(e^{iN\theta}f)-ie^{iN\theta}H(e^{-iN\theta}f)}{2}+\frac{P_{\pm N}}{2}.SN​(f)(θ)=2ie−iNθH(eiNθf)−ieiNθH(e−iNθf)​+2P±N​​.

Hence the study of the boundedness properties of the family of operators SN {S_{N}}SN​ reduces to the boundedness property of operators H {H}H and P±N {P_{\pm N}}P±N​.

The second question is concerned with a different summation method of Fourier series, and its connection to complex analysis. Here for each θ∈[0,2π] {\theta\in[0,2\pi]}θ∈[0,2π], the Fourier series is called Abel summable to f(θ) {f(\theta)}f(θ) if

∑n∈Zf∧(n)r∣n∣einθ→f(θ)\displaystyle \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f^{\wedge}(n)r^{|n|}e^{in\theta}\rightarrow f(\theta)n∈Z∑​f∧(n)r∣n∣einθ→f(θ)

as r→1 {r\rightarrow1}r→1. Similar to the symmetric partial sum, Abel summation can also be written as a convolution of f {f}f with a kernel. This time it is the Poisson kernel for the unit disk

f∗Pr (θ),\displaystyle f*\mathcal{P}_{r}\thinspace(\theta),f∗Pr​(θ),

where

Pr(θ)=∑n∈Zr∣n∣einθ=1−r21−2rcos⁡θ+r2.\displaystyle \mathcal{P}_{r}(\theta)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}r^{|n|}e^{in\theta}=\frac{1-r^{2}}{1-2r\cos\theta+r^{2}}.Pr​(θ)=n∈Z∑​r∣n∣einθ=1−2rcosθ+r21−r2​.

We remark that if for a.e. θ∈[0,2π] {\theta\in[0,2\pi]}θ∈[0,2π], a Fourier series is Abel summable and moreover, f∧(n)=0 {f^{\wedge}(n)=0}f∧(n)=0 for all n<0 {n<0}n<0, then f {f}f , originally defined on the unit circle, can be extended to a holomorphic function inside the unit disk, by

F(z)=∑n∈Zf∧(n)zn.\displaystyle F(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f^{\wedge}(n)z^{n}.F(z)=n∈Z∑​f∧(n)zn.

It is of interest that when the a.e. convergence holds. In sharp contrast to the symmetric partial sum method, it turns out that the result holds even for integrable functions. This is to be explained by the fact that the family of Poisson kernels, indexed in r {r}r, forms an approximations to the identity, while it is not the case for the Dirichlet kernels.

Now we ask the converse, that is, given a holomorphic function F {F}F in the unit disk, then under what conditions F {F}F will have radial limit on the circle, i.e.

lim⁡r→1−F(reiθ) exists for a.e. θ∈[0,2π]?\displaystyle \lim_{r\rightarrow1^{-}}F(re^{i\theta}) \text{ exists for a.e. } \theta\in [0,2\pi]?r→1−lim​F(reiθ) exists for a.e. θ∈[0,2π]?

Suppose F {F}F has the power series expansion ∑n=0∞anzn {\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n}z^{n}}∑n=0∞​an​zn. Now by Parseval's identity

∑n=0∞∣an∣2r2n=12π∫[0,2π]∣F(reiθ)∣2dθ,0≤r<1.\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|a_{n}|^{2}r^{2n}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{[0,2\pi]}|F(re^{i\theta})|^{2}d\theta, 0\leq r<1.n=0∑∞​∣an​∣2r2n=2π1​∫[0,2π]​∣F(reiθ)∣2dθ,0≤r<1.

Thus, assume that

sup⁡0≤r<1∫[0,2π]∣F(reiθ)∣2dθ<∞,(1) \displaystyle \sup_{0\leq r<1}\int_{[0,2\pi]}|F(re^{i\theta})|^{2}d\theta<\infty, (1)0≤r<1sup​∫[0,2π]​∣F(reiθ)∣2dθ<∞,(1)

so that the series ∑n=0∞∣an∣2 {\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|a_{n}|^{2}}∑n=0∞​∣an​∣2 converges to the above quantity, and thus has a corresponding L2 {L^{2}}L2 function F0(eiθ). {F_{0}(e^{i\theta}).}F0​(eiθ). Since L2([0,2π])⊂L1([0,2π]) {L^{2}([0,2\pi])\subset L^{1}([0,2\pi])}L2([0,2π])⊂L1([0,2π]), by the above paragraph we have the limit lim⁡r→1−F(reiθ) {\lim_{r\rightarrow1^{-}}F(re^{i\theta})}limr→1−​F(reiθ) exists for a.e. θ {\theta}θ. This result was obtained by Fatou.

The space of holomorphic functions on the unit disk satisfying the bound (1) is called the Hardy space H2(D) {H^2(\mathbb{D})}H2(D), with norm ∥F∥H2(D) {\|F\|_{H^{2}(\mathbb{D})}}∥F∥H2(D)​ defined to be the quantity on the LHS of (1). It can be identified with the closed subspace ℓ2(Z+) {\ell^{2}(\mathbb{Z}_{+})}ℓ2(Z+​) of the Hilbert space ℓ2(Z) {\ell^{2}(\mathbb{Z})}ℓ2(Z), or equivalently the space S {\mathcal{S}}S of square integrable functions on the cirlce whose Fourier coefficients vanish for n<0 {n<0}n<0. In view of this, define the orthogonal projection from L2([0,2π]) {L^{2}([0,2\pi])}L2([0,2π]) to S {\mathcal{S}}S, and write in the corresponding element in H2(D) {H^{2}(\mathbb{D})}H2(D)

P(f)(z):=∑n=0∞anzn.=∑n=0∞(12π∫[0,2π]f(eiθ)e−inθ dθ)zn=12π∫[0,2π]f(eiθ)∑n=0∞(e−iθz)n dθ=12πi∫S1f(ζ)ζ−z dζ,\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} P(f)(z): & = & \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n}z^{n}.\\ & = & \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{[0,2\pi]}f(e^{i\theta})e^{-in\theta}\thinspace d\theta\right)z^{n}\\ & = & \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{[0,2\pi]}f(e^{i\theta})\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(e^{-i\theta}z\right)^{n}\thinspace d\theta\\ & = & \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{S^{1}}\frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}\thinspace d\zeta, \end{array}P(f)(z):​====​∑n=0∞​an​zn.∑n=0∞​(2π1​∫[0,2π]​f(eiθ)e−inθdθ)zn2π1​∫[0,2π]​f(eiθ)∑n=0∞​(e−iθz)ndθ2πi1​∫S1​ζ−zf(ζ)​dζ,​

which turns out to be the Cauchy integral on the circle. On the other hand, notice that

P(f)(eiθ)=f(eiθ)+iH(f)(eiθ)2.(2) \displaystyle P(f)(e^{i\theta})=\frac{f(e^{i\theta})+iH(f)(e^{i\theta})}{2}. (2)P(f)(eiθ)=2f(eiθ)+iH(f)(eiθ)​.(2)

For this reason, H(f) {H(f)}H(f) is often called conjugate to f {f}f, and hence can be also identified the imaginary part of the Cauchy kernel of the unit circle

1i(ζ−z)dζ=ieiψdψi(eiψ−reiθ)=Pr(θ−ψ)dψ+dψ2+iQr(θ−ψ)dψ.\displaystyle \frac{1}{i(\zeta-z)}d\zeta=\frac{ie^{i\psi}d\psi}{i(e^{i\psi}-re^{i\theta})}=\mathcal{P}_{r}(\theta-\psi)d\psi+\frac{d\psi}{2}+i\mathcal{Q}_{r}(\theta-\psi)d\psi.i(ζ−z)1​dζ=i(eiψ−reiθ)ieiψdψ​=Pr​(θ−ψ)dψ+2dψ​+iQr​(θ−ψ)dψ.

Here Qr(θ) {Q_{r}(\theta)}Qr​(θ) is known as the conjugate Poisson kernel. In explicit form,

Qr(θ−ψ)=rsin⁡(θ−ψ)1−2rcos⁡θ+r2→12cot⁡(θ−ψ2)\displaystyle \mathcal{Q}_{r}(\theta-\psi)=\frac{r\sin(\theta-\psi)}{1-2r\cos\theta+r^{2}}\rightarrow\frac{1}{2}\cot(\frac{\theta-\psi}{2})Qr​(θ−ψ)=1−2rcosθ+r2rsin(θ−ψ)​→21​cot(2θ−ψ​)

as r→1− {r\rightarrow1^{-}}r→1−. Unlike Poisson's kernel, it is not absolutely integrable, thus called "singular'', near the diagonal θ=ψ {\theta=\psi}θ=ψ, but note that cot⁡(x) {\cot(x)}cot(x) is an odd function on [−π,π] {[-\pi,\pi]}[−π,π], which is one manifestation of the {cancellation property} for such singular integral operators.

Now we turn to the analogous results of the above for functions on the real line, where the unit disk is replaced by the upper half space R+2:={(x,y)∈R2:y>0} {\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2}:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:y>0\}}R+2​:={(x,y)∈R2:y>0}. Starting with a function F0∧∈L2(0,∞) {F_{0}^{\wedge}\in L^{2}(0,\infty)}F0∧​∈L2(0,∞), define its Laplace transform to be

F(x+iy)=∫[0,∞)F0∧(ξ)e2πiξz dξ,(3) \displaystyle F(x+iy)=\int_{[0,\infty)}F_{0}^{\wedge}(\xi)e^{2\pi i\xi z}\thinspace d\xi, (3)F(x+iy)=∫[0,∞)​F0∧​(ξ)e2πiξzdξ,(3)

which can be viewed as an "integral version'' of Abel summation of the Fourier series ∑n≥0f∧(n) {\sum_{n\geq0}f^{\wedge}(n)}∑n≥0​f∧(n). (The analogue for ∑n∈Zf∧(n) {\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f^{\wedge}(n)}∑n∈Z​f∧(n) will be given by ∫Rf∧(ξ)e−2π∣ξ∣ye2πixξ dξ {\int_{\mathbb{R}}f^{\wedge}(\xi)e^{-2\pi|\xi|y}e^{2\pi ix\xi}\thinspace d\xi}∫R​f∧(ξ)e−2π∣ξ∣ye2πixξdξ.) Since for any δ>0 {\delta>0}δ>0, if y≥δ {y\geq\delta}y≥δ, the integral has the uniform bound

∫[0,∞)∣F0∧(ξ)e2πiξz∣ dξ≤(∫[0,∞)∣F0∧(ξ)∣2 dξ)1/2(∫[0,∞)e−4πξδ dξ)1/2,\displaystyle \int_{[0,\infty)}|F_{0}^{\wedge}(\xi)e^{2\pi i\xi z}|\thinspace d\xi\leq\left(\int_{[0,\infty)}|F_{0}^{\wedge}(\xi)|^{2}\thinspace d\xi\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-4\pi\xi\delta}\thinspace d\xi\right)^{1/2},∫[0,∞)​∣F0∧​(ξ)e2πiξz∣dξ≤(∫[0,∞)​∣F0∧​(ξ)∣2dξ)1/2(∫[0,∞)​e−4πξδdξ)1/2,

so F {F}F is in fact holomorphic in R+2 {\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2}}R+2​. Plancherel's identity implies that

∫R∣F(x+iy)∣2 dx=∫[0,∞)∣F0∧(ξ)∣2e−4πξy dξ≤∥F0∧∥L2(0,∞)2\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x+iy)|^{2}\thinspace dx=\int_{[0,\infty)}|F_{0}^{\wedge}(\xi)|^{2}e^{-4\pi\xi y}\thinspace d\xi\leq\|F_{0}^{\wedge}\|_{L^{2}(0,\infty)}^{2}∫R​∣F(x+iy)∣2dx=∫[0,∞)​∣F0∧​(ξ)∣2e−4πξydξ≤∥F0∧​∥L2(0,∞)2​

and by the monotone convergence theorem

sup⁡y>0∫R∣F(x+iy)∣2 dx=∥F0∧∥L2(0,∞)2.\displaystyle \sup_{y>0}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x+iy)|^{2}\thinspace dx=\|F_{0}^{\wedge}\|_{L^{2}(0,\infty)}^{2}.y>0sup​∫R​∣F(x+iy)∣2dx=∥F0∧​∥L2(0,∞)2​.

As before, the Hardy space H2(R+2) {H^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2})}H2(R+2​) is defined to be the space of holomorphic functions on R+2 {\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2}}R+2​ satisfying the condition

sup⁡y>0∫R∣F(x+iy)∣2 dx<∞,\displaystyle \sup_{y>0}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x+iy)|^{2}\thinspace dx<\infty,y>0sup​∫R​∣F(x+iy)∣2dx<∞,

and equipped with the norm ∥F∥H2(R+2) {\|F\|_{H^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2})}}∥F∥H2(R+2​)​ to be the above quantity.

Given such a function F {F}F with suitable decaying property, via a contour integration argument, its inverse Laplace transform satisfies, for any y1,y2>0 {y_{1},y_{2}>0}y1​,y2​>0.

∫RF(x+iy1)e−2πiξ(x+iy1) dx=∫RF(x+iy2)e−2πiξ(x+iy2) dx.\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x+iy_{1})e^{-2\pi i\xi(x+iy_{1})}\thinspace dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(x+iy_{2})e^{-2\pi i\xi(x+iy_{2})}\thinspace dx.∫R​F(x+iy1​)e−2πiξ(x+iy1​)dx=∫R​F(x+iy2​)e−2πiξ(x+iy2​)dx.

In other words, there is a deck transformation rule

Fy1∧(ξ)e2πy1ξ=Fy2∧(ξ)e2πy2ξ.\displaystyle F_{y_{1}}^{\wedge}(\xi)e^{2\pi y_{1}\xi}=F_{y_{2}}^{\wedge}(\xi)e^{2\pi y_{2}\xi}.Fy1​∧​(ξ)e2πy1​ξ=Fy2​∧​(ξ)e2πy2​ξ.

A limiting argument shows this it is true for all F∈H2(R+2) {F\in H^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2})}F∈H2(R+2​). Hence the function F0∧(ξ):=Fy∧(ξ)e2πyξ {F_{0}^{\wedge}(\xi):=F_{y}^{\wedge}(\xi)e^{2\pi y\xi}}F0∧​(ξ):=Fy∧​(ξ)e2πyξ is well defined, and by Plancherel's identity

∫R∣F(x+iy)∣2 dx=∫R∣F0∧(ξ)∣2e−4πyξ dx.\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb{R}}|F(x+iy)|^{2}\thinspace dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F_{0}^{\wedge}(\xi)|^{2}e^{-4\pi y\xi}\thinspace dx.∫R​∣F(x+iy)∣2dx=∫R​∣F0∧​(ξ)∣2e−4πyξdx.

Thus,

∥F∥H2(R+2)=∫R∣F0∧(ξ)∣2 dx\displaystyle \|F\|_{H^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2})}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}|F_{0}^{\wedge}(\xi)|^{2}\thinspace dx∥F∥H2(R+2​)​=∫R​∣F0∧​(ξ)∣2dx

and H2(R+2) {H^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2})}H2(R+2​) can be identified with the Hilbert space L2(0,∞) {L^{2}(0,\infty)}L2(0,∞) via (3).

It then follows that F {F}F has boundary values F0 {F_{0}}F0​, the inverse Fourier transform of F0∧ {F_{0}^{\wedge}}F0∧​, in the L2 {L^{2}}L2 sense. It also holds a.e., once we have the Poisson integral representation

F(x+iy)=∫[0,∞)F0∧(ξ)e2πiξz dξ=∫RF0(x−t)Py(t) dt\displaystyle F(x+iy)=\int_{[0,\infty)}F_{0}^{\wedge}(\xi)e^{2\pi i\xi z}\thinspace d\xi=\int_{\mathbb{R}}F_{0}(x-t)\mathcal{P}_{y}(t)\thinspace dtF(x+iy)=∫[0,∞)​F0∧​(ξ)e2πiξzdξ=∫R​F0​(x−t)Py​(t)dt

or more generally,

∫Rf∧(ξ)e−2π∣ξ∣ye2πixξ dξ=∫Rf(x−t)Py(t) dt\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb{R}}f^{\wedge}(\xi)e^{-2\pi|\xi|y}e^{2\pi ix\xi}\thinspace d\xi=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x-t)\mathcal{P}_{y}(t)\thinspace dt∫R​f∧(ξ)e−2π∣ξ∣ye2πixξdξ=∫R​f(x−t)Py​(t)dt

where Py(x)=1πyx2+y2 {\mathcal{P}_{y}(x)=\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}}}Py​(x)=π1​x2+y2y​ is the Poisson kernel for the upper half space. To see this, define the Cauchy kernel for y>0 {y>0}y>0

C(x+iy)=∫Re2πi∣ξ∣z dξ=∫R2χ[0,∞)e2πiξz dξ=iπz.\displaystyle C(x+iy)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{2\pi i|\xi|z}\thinspace d\xi=\int_{\mathbb{R}}2\chi_{[0,\infty)}e^{2\pi i\xi z}\thinspace d\xi=\frac{i}{\pi z}.C(x+iy)=∫R​e2πi∣ξ∣zdξ=∫R​2χ[0,∞)​e2πiξzdξ=πzi​.

Then

Py(x)=∫Re−2π∣ξ∣ye2πixξ dξ=∫[0,∞)e−2πξye2πixξ dξ+∫[0,∞)e−2πξye−2πixξ dξ=12(C(x+iy)+C(−x+iy))=1πyx2+y2.\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} \mathcal{P}_{y}(x) & = & \int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-2\pi|\xi|y}e^{2\pi ix\xi}\thinspace d\xi\\ & = & \int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-2\pi\xi y}e^{2\pi ix\xi}\thinspace d\xi+\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{-2\pi\xi y}e^{-2\pi ix\xi}\thinspace d\xi\\ & = & \frac{1}{2}(C(x+iy)+C(-x+iy))\\ & = & \frac{1}{\pi}\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}}. \end{array}Py​(x)​====​∫R​e−2π∣ξ∣ye2πixξdξ∫[0,∞)​e−2πξye2πixξdξ+∫[0,∞)​e−2πξye−2πixξdξ21​(C(x+iy)+C(−x+iy))π1​x2+y2y​.​

Notice that for y>0 {y>0}y>0

iπz=Py(x)+iQy(x)\displaystyle \frac{i}{\pi z}=\mathcal{P}_{y}(x)+i\mathcal{Q}_{y}(x)πzi​=Py​(x)+iQy​(x)

where Qy(x)=1πxx2+y2 {\mathcal{Q}_{y}(x)=\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}}}Qy​(x)=π1​x2+y2x​ is the conjugate Poisson kernel. We would like to know what happens when y→0 {y\rightarrow0}y→0. This is the clearest in terms of multipliers. We have, corresponding to the above,

2χ[0,∞)e−2πξy=e−2π∣ξ∣y+1isign(ξ)e−2π∣ξ∣y\displaystyle 2\chi_{[0,\infty)}e^{-2\pi\xi y}=e^{-2\pi|\xi|y}+\frac{1}{i}\text{sign}(\xi)e^{-2\pi|\xi|y}2χ[0,∞)​e−2πξy=e−2π∣ξ∣y+i1​sign(ξ)e−2π∣ξ∣y
